page: UpCloud CLOUDNATIVE-32xCPU-384GB is a memory-optimized cloud server powered by the AMD EPYC 7542 processor on the x86_64 architecture. Delivered via KVM virtualization, it features 32 shared virtual cores (with 32 physical cores at 1 thread per core) clocked at a base frequency of 2.0 GHz. The processor includes 64 KB of L1d cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache, along with cryptographic acceleration flags including AES and SHA-NI, though it lacks AVX-512 extensions. The server is provisioned with 384.0 GB of RAM, resulting in a substantial 12.0 GB of memory per core. It includes no bundled local storage, no GPUs, and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results highlight solid throughput across multi-threaded operations and data processing tasks. The instance scored 17,094.0 points in Geekbench multi-core and 1,980.0 in Geekbench single-core, both registering in the top 25% of measured systems. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression also demonstrated top-quartile performance at 228.74 GB/sec. Memory subsystem testing revealed an uncached large-block read speed of 131.44 GB/sec and write bandwidth of 82.64 GB/sec, supporting steady database and caching performance, such as 35.27 million operations per second in Redis SET tests.

Single-core compute tasks reveal performance tradeoffs. The stress-ng single-core benchmark landed in the bottom 10% with a score of 748.19, and single-threaded gzip compression rated weak at 23.67 GB/sec. However, multi-core stress-ng reached 21,669.29, and the PassMark CPU score hit 42,176.07, positioning general multi-threaded execution firmly in the mid-range. For language model execution, prompt processing on a 7B model ran at 92.06 tokens/sec with generation at 10.56 tokens/sec, while a 70B model processed prompts at 9.24 tokens/sec.

The 12:1 memory-to-core ratio delivers strong cost efficiency for scale-up footprints that prioritize memory capacity over extreme single-threaded CPU speed. UpCloud CLOUDNATIVE-32xCPU-384GB is primarily suited for large in-memory caching layers, Redis clusters, relational databases requiring expansive buffer pools, analytics engines, and high-concurrency batch processing workloads.
